title: A way out
hook: whoever is mindful of Allah, He makes a way out and provides from where he never expects (65:2–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: parting with kindness, from the surah named divorce. Your line was part with kindness. Did something end a little gentler than it might have? Day six hundred thirty-three.

Some problems have walls on every side. The rent and the paycheck don't meet. The diagnosis has no good option. The family fight has gone on so long nobody remembers how it started. You've run the math at two in the morning, and every road ends in the same brick. Many Muslims, in exactly that spot, reach for one line from the Qur'an. It isn't in a chapter about miracles or battles. It sits right in the middle of yesterday's surah, between the rules for divorce.

Surah at-Talaq, verses two and three. In Pickthall's translation: "And whosoever keepeth his duty to Allah, Allah will appoint a way out for him, And will provide for him from (a quarter) whence he hath no expectation." Keeping your duty is Pickthall's phrase for taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, living as someone who knows they're seen. The way out is one Arabic word, makhraj. It comes from the root for going out, the same root as the word for an exit. Not a cure for every problem. An exit. And the second promise is stranger: provision from where you never expected. Not from the road you were staring at. From somewhere off the map. Then the verse goes on: whoever puts their trust in Allah, He is enough for them. Now notice where this sits. The verses before and after are about the waiting period, the house, the witnesses, the money owed when a marriage ends. Commentators have long pointed out that this is no accident. Divorce is one of the places people feel most trapped: by money, by children, by fear of being alone. And right there, in the middle of the rules, the Qur'an breaks in with hope. It doesn't promise the exit will be the one you wanted. It doesn't say when. It says the walls are not the whole story. Many Muslims memorize these two verses and repeat them when a problem has no visible door. They don't treat it as a trick to make the problem vanish. They treat it as a way to keep doing the right thing while they wait for the door they can't see yet.
screen: `TAQWA: LIVING AS ONE WHO IS SEEN.`
`HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE RULES.`

segments.voice: The practice: trust with a hard problem. Sit, and let one real problem come to mind, the one with walls. Don't solve it. Just name it, in one sentence, silently. Then picture it as a room, and notice you've been staring at the same wall. Let your attention drift to the corners you haven't looked at. If you pray, you can hold the verse there: a way out, from where you never expected. If you don't, just breathe with the problem without pushing on it. The bell holds the time.
A way out. Makhraj, an exit, promised in 65:2 to whoever keeps their duty to Allah, with provision from where they never expected. Today's word.
Your line: a way out comes. Today, when you hit a wall, do the next right thing anyway, and keep one eye on the corner you weren't watching. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize 65:2–3, sometimes called the verse of the way out, and recite it in times of debt, illness or family trouble, alongside the promise that whoever trusts in Allah, He is enough for them.
